options.label: A
options.text: The fixer brings along the documentation of every docspec its change reaches by either path, editing each sentence the fix made false and adding each public element the fix added, and the verifier checks both; cost: every certification fix that changes observable behavior reads the surface intent and the docspec index.

options.label: B
options.text: After the fix loop, certification re-runs the documentation pass of each docspec a fix reached, and the pass's findings join a further fix round; cost: one more pass per reached docspec, a longer loop, and a departure from the rule that neither loop re-reads what a fix changed.

options.label: C
options.text: Certification fixes leave documentation alone, and the completion report lists each docspec a fix reached for the next sprint; cost: the sprint's commit lands with stale documentation, so the story needs a delta.

problem:
When sprint certification fixes a defect and the fix changes something a user can observe, such as a flag, a message, or an output format, no agent brings along the documentation that describes it, so the sprint's commit ships documentation of the behavior before the fix. That breaks the promise that each change brings the documentation it affects along in the same change, so the documentation at any commit describes the product at that commit ([story:keep-documentation-current](.ok-planner/design/stories/keep-documentation-current.md)).

The mechanism. A docspec is the owner's declaration of one kind of documentation: where it lives, and which parts of the project it describes ([concept:docspec](.ok-planner/design/concepts/docspec.md)). A change reaches a docspec two ways ([artifact-definitions.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L172-L173)): it touches a file the docspec's references name, or it touches a file the surface intent names as declaring a class of public element the docspec must list in full. Certification's review runs its documentation passes once, before any fix ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L101)). That pass ([sprint-pass.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md#L28)) covers both reach paths and reports each public element the documentation omits. After the review, the fixer is told 'Change nothing the defect does not need' ([fix.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/fix.md#L24)) and has no step that reads a docspec, and the verifier checks 'the change, and only the change' ([verify.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/verify.md#L9)). The next `/plan-sprint` reconciles only changes made after the sprint's closing commit ([decision:closing-commit-baseline](.ok-planner/design/decisions/closing-commit-baseline.md)), so nothing later catches the stale text. A reader of the documentation at that commit sees it.

The state of play. A kept fix in the certification run converge-2026-10-17T021110 widened the rule for which prose is in review: documentation a sprint's change reaches, its certification fixes included, is now in review ([coding-rules.md:PROSE-SCOPE-RULE](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_converge/coding-rules.md#L38-L61), restated at [converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L40)). So the documentation is in scope, but no agent reads it after a fix. A second fix gave the fixer and the verifier a documentation step over the references path only. The confirm driver sent it back because it missed the declaring-file path and caught only sentences a fix made false, not public elements a fix added, and the run backed it out. The decision on who writes documentation ([decision:sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/sprints-write-the-documentation.md)) says certification reviews each touched documentation against its docspec and the change, and says nothing of certification fixes. Three sibling issues bear on the same rule and are best ruled together: converge-commits-leave-documentation-behind, for plain runs; listed-class-change-reach, on how a declaring-file change reaches a docspec; and out-of-band-review-misses-declaring-files.

The ruling decides how a certification fix brings along the documentation its change reaches.

recommendation.text:
A certification fixer whose change alters behavior a user can observe brings along the documentation of every docspec the change reaches, by either reach path: it edits each sentence the fix made false and adds each public element the fix added, following the one statement of the reach rule and the listing rule the suite already carries rather than a second copy. The verifier checks the documentation as part of the change. Rule listed-class-change-reach in the same sprint, so the declaring-file path means the same thing here as at planning.

Rationale: the documentation decision has the agent who writes a change write its documentation after the code, and has review judge both; A gives a certification fix that same shape, and keeps the fix loop the decision on finding and fixing defines, where the verifier reads only the change, which now includes its documentation. B reuses the review's check but re-reads after the fix loop, which that decision rejected for code, and needs that decision amended. C gives up the story's 'at any commit' for every sprint whose certification changes behavior. The backed-out attempt failed on its scope, one reach path and false sentences only, not on its shape, and A closes both gaps. The flip case: if the fixer and verifier cannot apply the listing rule by reference and A would copy the documentation pass's listing procedure into the fix and verify prompts, B's single check is the better call despite the amendment.

title: A sprint-certification fix lands with the documentation it affects still describing the old behavior

options.label: A
options.text: The return gives one line per approved corpus delta, saying whether it landed at build, landed by certification, or stuck; cost: a longer return on a sprint with many deltas.

options.label: B
options.text: The story is met by the C3 defect lines and the repository check of contract item 1, and the return names a delta only where one failed; cost: the owner reads delivery of the deltas from silence, which a return that skipped the comparison would also show.

options.label: C
options.text: The return gives one summary line for the deltas: how many it compared, how many had landed at build, how many certification landed, and how many stuck, naming by artifact each delta certification landed and each that stuck; cost: one line, and the owner sees each landed delta only as a count.

problem:
Sprint certification's return never states that the sprint's approved corpus deltas landed, and names a delta only where one did not, so an owner reading the return learns that a delta was delivered only from silence, against [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md), which promises 'a way to know, when a sprint closes, whether what I approved was delivered, so that "done" means the same thing for every sprint'.

The mechanism. An approved sprint carries two kinds of content: work items, which builders turn into code, and corpus deltas, the final-form text of each concept, story, decision, docspec, or surface intent the sprint changes. Certification's alignment pass compares each delta with its artifact byte for byte ([converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/sprint-pass.md#L27)), and a delta that did not land becomes a C3 defect, which the fix loop lands by copying the delta's body into place ([converge/prompts/fix.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/fix.md#L27)). The return's `sprint` field ([converge/SKILL.md:The return](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L149)) gives one line per work item and taken improvement, saying whether each works end to end, and lines for the docspecs judged, the behavior changes, the stories driven, and the checks. It has no line for deltas. A C3 defect shows only in the `fixed` field, counted by sprint class ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L150)), or as stuck. The completion report carries the return, so the report is silent on deltas too.

The state of play. The repository check is built: completion contract item 1 ([plan-sprint/sprint-document.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L268-L272)) requires every corpus to match every delta, and [decision:final-form-deltas](.ok-planner/design/decisions/final-form-deltas.md) makes that comparison certification's job. The gap is only what the owner reads: a sprint whose approved content is mostly deltas gets a return that speaks for its work items and not for its deltas.

The ruling decides whether certification's return states the deltas' delivery, and in how much detail.

recommendation.text:
Certification's return carries one line for the sprint's corpus deltas: how many it compared, how many had landed at build, how many it landed itself, and how many stuck, naming by artifact each delta it landed and each that stuck.

Rationale: the story asks for a way to know whether what the owner approved was delivered, and [decision:final-form-deltas](.ok-planner/design/decisions/final-form-deltas.md) holds that restricting corpus change to the delta gives the sign-off its weight, so the deltas are half of what the owner approves. The return already states delivery positively for each work item. Option B leaves the other half to silence, and silence reads the same whether the comparison ran or not. Option C states that the comparison ran, and on how many deltas, at the cost of one line, and it names the deltas worth a look: the ones the build missed and the ones that stuck. Option A's line per delta repeats, for every delta that landed, what the count already says. Flip case: if the owner wants each artifact named to check against the sprint they approved, as on a sprint with few deltas, option A gives that at the cost of length.

title: Sprint certification's return says nothing of the sprint's corpus deltas unless one failed

options.label: A
options.text: [decision:sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/sprints-write-the-documentation.md) admits a `/converge` fix that brings along the documentation its change reaches, and the run's scope rule, fix, and verify steps widen to match; cost: every plain run reads the docspecs and the surface intent and edits documentation, by whatever mechanism the ruling on certification-fix-leaves-documentation settles.

options.label: B
options.text: [story:keep-documentation-current](.ok-planner/design/stories/keep-documentation-current.md) scopes 'at any commit' to the commits a sprint makes, and a plain run's commits wait for the next reconcile; cost: the documentation is stale from a plain run's commit until the next sprint, and the story promises less.

options.label: C
options.text: As B, and a plain run's owner list files an issue naming each docspec a committed fix reached, so the gap is recorded at the commit instead of found at reconcile; cost: the documentation is still stale until the next sprint, and each reached docspec costs one intake write.

problem:
A plain `/converge` run, in drive, analysis, or defects mode, commits product fixes and leaves the documentation those fixes affect as it was. That breaks the promise of [story:keep-documentation-current](.ok-planner/design/stories/keep-documentation-current.md): 'each change to my product bring the documentation it affects along in the same change, so that the documentation a reader finds at any commit describes the product at that commit.'

The mechanism: such a run fixes product code and ends with an offer to commit the fixes. Its prose scope rule, [{{PROSE-SCOPE-RULE}}](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_converge/coding-rules.md#L38-L61), puts documentation in review only in a run that certifies a sprint: 'Anywhere else, and in a run that certifies no sprint, file no finding on it and edit none of it.' The rule follows [decision:sprints-write-the-documentation](.ok-planner/design/decisions/sprints-write-the-documentation.md), whose Choice reads 'Of the suite's runs, only a sprint writes a project's documentation' and 'Outside these, documentation stays as it is.' A docspec is the owner's declaration of one kind of documentation and the parts of the project it describes ([concept:docspec](.ok-planner/design/concepts/docspec.md)). So a fix that changes a flag, a message, or an output that a docspec's documentation describes lands in a commit whose documentation still describes the old behavior, and every reader of that documentation sees the old behavior until something catches it up.

The state of play: a catch-up path exists. The next `/plan-sprint`'s reconcile flags 'Code or corpus a docspec references, changed outside a sprint' and adds a work item or an issue ([decision:out-of-band-documentation-reconciled](.ok-planner/design/decisions/out-of-band-documentation-reconciled.md)). So the documentation is wrong from the plain run's commit until the next sprint, and no longer. The story and the decision cannot both hold for a plain run's commits, and either fix changes the corpus, so no review run could make it: converge-2026-10-17T021110 left it alone. problem:
`/plan-sprint` writes the sprint file at its Draft step and writes no mark at Approval, so a draft a session leaves when it dies before approval looks the same as an approved sprint. That breaks the promise of [story:plan-a-sprint](.ok-planner/design/stories/plan-a-sprint.md) of 'a signed-off, self-sufficient sprint, so that any executor can realize my intent', and the rule of [decision:final-form-deltas](.ok-planner/design/decisions/final-form-deltas.md) that only applying an approved sprint's deltas changes what the corpus commits to.

The mechanism: [Draft](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md#L95-L97) writes the sprint to `.ok-planner/sprints/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md` from [the sprint template](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md), and the steps after it refine that file in place. [Approval](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md#L196-L200) says 'It is not final until the owner approves.' [Terminal](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md#L202-L214) records the issue promotions and hands the owner the goal line, and writes nothing into the sprint. The template carries no approval field. No executor checks approval: a grep of the `/converge` skill, its sprint-review prompt, and the drain loop finds none, and `issues promote <id> --sprint <file>` accepted a file holding only a title and an Intent heading. So an executor (the `/goal` line, a drain of build tasks, `/converge sprint`) pointed at a draft applies deltas and builds work the owner never approved, and nothing warns the owner or the executor.

The state of play: the intake is safe. Promotions land only at Terminal, after approval ([SKILL.md:154](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md#L154)), so a dead session leaves its issues open with their rulings kept. Only the sprint file is ambiguous. The corpus says a sprint 'owns approved intent' ([concept:sprint](.ok-planner/design/concepts/sprint.md)) and says nothing about how an executor tells approved intent from a draft. A precedent exists for a lifecycle mark on the sprint file: [decision:closing-commit-baseline](.ok-planner/design/decisions/closing-commit-baseline.md) stamps an archived sprint's frontmatter with its closing commit.

The ruling decides whether the story owes an executor a way to tell an approved sprint from a draft, and in what form.

A draft that an executor cannot tell from an approved sprint undoes both, so A leaves the harm in place. The mark follows the precedent of the closing-commit stamp, which records a sprint's lifecycle on the file itself. The refusal sits where the harm happens, at every executor, while C protects only an executor that never sees the draft name, and moves every planning reference at the last step. The flip case: if executors in practice start only from the goal line that Terminal hands over, which a dead session never prints, A's risk is small enough that the template field and the refusals cost more than they save.

The flip case: if the owner wants each docspec to state in one file everything that reaches it, auditable by eye, and accepts a review check that its References cover its listed classes' declaring files, B is the call; C adds churn without closing B's gap.

[story:reference-names-the-public-surface](.ok-planner/design/stories/reference-names-the-public-surface.md) owes a reference that names 'every element I made public and no element I kept internal'.

The mechanism: such an element reaches a reference only where some `## Lists` bullet names its class. If `## Lists` may name only classes public by default, the element reaches no reference, and nothing notices, since certification checks a reference only against the classes its docspec lists. If `## Lists` may name an internal class, the builder lists only that class's public exceptions.

The state of play: a fixer built the second reading. The docspec definition's [## Lists bullet](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L173) reads 'a class whose rule makes its members public, or one whose exceptions make a member public', and lists 'for a class its rule keeps internal, only the members its exceptions make public'. The sibling issue listed-class-change-reach decides how a change to a listed class reaches its docspec, and either reading here feeds it.

The ruling decides how a public exception of an internal class reaches a reference.

recommendation.text:
A reference docspec's `## Lists` may name any class that has public members, whether the class's rule makes them public or its exceptions do, and the reference lists exactly the class's public members as the surface intent decides them, as built. The docspec concept says so: a reference docspec names the classes whose public members its documentation must list in full.

Rationale: the surface intent is the one document that decides each element's status, by class rules and named exceptions, and a docspec that names a class and defers to the intent for its members keeps that one decider. B adds a second listing rule beside `## Lists`, and C bends the intent's form to fit the docspec and fails silently until the owner restructures the intent. Under this reading the story's 'every element I made public' holds for an exception by the same mechanism as for any public class, and the reach the ruling on listed-class-change-reach settles covers it with no special case. The flip case: if owners in practice make so few members of internal classes public that a `## Lists` naming an internal class confuses more readers than it serves, C's explicit public class is the cleaner call, paired with a planning check that flags a public exception no listed class covers.

title: Whether a reference docspec may list a class the surface intent keeps internal

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Payload scripts carry no annotations, and the build rule and the project's rules say so; a story realized only in a payload script is cited from a repository-only site, such as a check, or not at all; cost: the annotation grep does not find the code that realizes the story.

problem:
No code site in this repository cites the story that the owner can see and overturn every call made in their absence ([story:veto-calls-made-in-my-absence](.ok-planner/design/stories/veto-calls-made-in-my-absence.md)). The build rule says each story implemented in code carries a `@story:` annotation at the site that realizes it ([sprint-document.md step 8](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L160-L163)), and the citation rule says whoever consults an artifact while working on a file leaves the annotation ([decision:code-cites-design](.ok-planner/design/decisions/code-cites-design.md)).

The mechanism. This repository is the suite's source. A payload script is a script the suite copies into every consumer project on true-up, such as the task tracker. The story's realizing site is the tracker's calls table, [tasks:calls_table](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tasks#L1297); the calls rows in the converge skill's return and in the planner's step 13 are payload too. The project's check [checks/materialized-standalone](checks/materialized-standalone#L47) copies each payload script into a bare git repository and lints it there, where no citation tag is declared, so any `@story:` comment in a payload script fails the lint's comment rule. The check also refuses, in every markdown payload, any citation that resolves in this repository's corpus. The check stands because a consumer's lint knows only the tags that consumer declares ([concept:citation-tag](.ok-planner/design/concepts/citation-tag.md)), and a consumer's corpus holds none of the suite's slugs. Sprint 2026-10-16-docspec-and-audit-backout planned the annotation on the calls table, and the builder left it out because the check refuses it.

The state of play. No payload script carries a citation; the true-up core, which runs from the plugin and is never copied, carries 101. True-up already transforms what it copies: [true-up:render](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L141) rewrites skill prefixes and shared paths and appends the stamp. No rule says whether a payload script may carry a citation this repository resolves and a consumer never sees. A missing annotation costs navigation only, so no accept-list harm is at stake.

The ruling decides where the project cites a design artifact that only a payload script realizes.

recommendation.text:
Let a payload script carry a design citation that resolves in this repository, and have true-up strip each citation comment line from a payload script when it copies the script into a project, so a consumer's copy carries none. The standalone check lints that stripped copy rather than the source. Markdown payloads keep refusing citations, since a skill's text may show the annotation syntax to a consumer. The tracker's calls table then carries the story's annotation.

Rationale: the corpus makes the annotation grep the index of where each artifact is load-bearing, and in this repository most load-bearing code is payload, so C leaves the grep blind where the suite's behavior lives and turns the build rule into one no builder can meet there. B keeps the index but hands it to consumers who cannot resolve it. A keeps both: this repository resolves every annotation, and a consumer sees none. Its cost is small, because true-up already renders every file it copies, and stripping comment lines in the one citation grammar is one more rewrite in a step that exists. The flip case: if a consumer or a check needs a vendored script to match its source line for line apart from the stamp, the strip breaks that, and C, with the annotation on a repository-only check, becomes the better call.

title: A story realized only in a payload script has no site the project's check lets carry its citation

options.label: A
options.text: A plain run meets the story through the shown table and the intake, which any person files into, and the return keeps asking nothing; cost: the owner turns a disagreement into an issue by hand, and nothing ties that issue to the call's row.

options.label: B
options.text: A plain run's return asks which rows of its calls table the owner vetoes and files one issue per vetoed row, as sprint mode's close does; cost: a run meant to end with nothing to settle ends with a question.

options.label: C
options.text: The return asks nothing, and the archive-and-commit offer, which already waits for the owner, also takes vetoes in the same answer; cost: one answer carries two acts, and the two modes close differently.

problem:
In drive, analysis, and defects mode, `/converge` ends by printing a table of the calls it made without the owner and then asks the owner nothing, so a call the owner disagrees with is shown once and committed with the run. The story that the owner can see every call made in their absence and overturn one they disagree with ([story:veto-calls-made-in-my-absence](.ok-planner/design/stories/veto-calls-made-in-my-absence.md)) gets its first half and not its second.

The mechanism. A call here is a judgment an agent made alone: a fixer's decline or duplicate, a failure sorted as not owed, a rejected report. The skill's return ([converge/SKILL.md:The return](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L143)) lists one row per such call, then says the block 'asks the owner nothing' and offers only to archive and commit the run ([converge/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L156)). The run files an issue only for a decline or duplicate no verifier checked, so a verified decline, a rejected report, or a not-owed failure reaches no record. To overturn one, the owner must notice it in the return and file an issue by hand, and nothing ties that issue to the row. Sprint mode differs: after certification, the planner's close presents the same table, asks which rows the owner vetoes, and files one issue per vetoed row with the owner's words as its ruling ([sprint-document.md step 13](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md#L209-L235)).

The state of play. The owner's ruling on the issue converge-calls-reach-owner-as-counts put a plain run's calls into the same table and says 'At the close, the session presents the table, and the owner vetoes any row they disagree with.' That sentence reads either as covering a plain run or as speaking of sprint certification alone. Against a veto step stands the run's commitment to end at a state the owner can read without waiting on them ([decision:converge-finds-then-fixes](.ok-planner/design/decisions/converge-finds-then-fixes.md)), though the return's archive-and-commit offer already waits for the owner's word.

The ruling decides whether a plain run's return offers the overturn itself.

recommendation.text:
A plain run's return presents its calls table and asks which rows the owner vetoes, in the same closing exchange as the archive-and-commit offer, and files one issue per vetoed row with the owner's words as its ruling, as sprint certification's close does. A run that made no calls asks nothing new.

Rationale: the story promises an overturn, not only a view, and the owner's ruling on calls already says the owner vetoes rows at the close; reading that sentence as covering a plain run gives both modes one close, which the project's rule of one idiom per job asks for. A leaves the overturn to a hand-filed issue that names no row, the gap the story exists to close. C folds the veto into the commit answer, so one reply carries two acts and the two modes close in two shapes. B adds no wait the run does not already have: the fixes are done before the return, and the commit already waits for the owner's word. The flip case: if plain runs are meant to run with no one at the close, such as on a schedule, the question would sit unanswered, and A, with the table written into a record the owner reads later, would serve better.

title: A plain /converge run shows its calls table but gives the owner no step to overturn a call

options.label: A
options.text: A rewrite of a stamped suite file that carries an uncommitted or staged-only change counts as destructive: true-up copies the working file into the archive first, and the plan asks the owner once; cost: a question on an upgrade where the owner edited a file whose stamp says not to, and a git-state check on every stale file.

options.label: B
options.text: The suite states that a stamped file's uncommitted edits are discarded on rewrite, and the story narrows the work it protects to files the owner owns; cost: an owner who edits a stamped file loses the edit with no notice.

options.label: C
options.text: True-up rewrites with no question but copies the uncommitted working file into the archive first and names it in its report; cost: the archive grows with copies the owner may not want, and an archive move without consent departs from the rule that every archive move is destructive.

options.label: D
options.text: True-up rewrites with no question and names each discarded uncommitted change by path in its report; cost: the edit is still lost, only named.

problem:
True-up, the suite's upgrade pass, overwrites a suite-owned file that still carries its stamp even where the owner has an uncommitted or staged-only edit in it, with no question and no copy, so the edit is lost. That breaks the promise that upgrading the suite never costs the owner work they wrote ([story:true-up-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/true-up-project-estate.md)).

The mechanism. Where a file on disk differs from the rendering the suite carries, [true-up:materialize_steps](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L4007) queues a rewrite and never asks git whether the difference is committed. The git-state check [true-up:uncommitted](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L570) runs only for removals, through [true-up:removal_split](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L609), and for archive steps. A person who appends lines to a stamped file leaves the stamp in place, so the rule that decides which steps need the owner's consent counts the rewrite as safe: it calls a step destructive where it 'rewrites a file a person edited, which is every file but a suite-owned file that still carries its stamp or its fixed content' ([decision:true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps](.ok-planner/design/decisions/true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps.md)). The plan then holds no destructive step, and `/ok` runs it with no question. The suite's ownership rule promises that true-up 'never discards uncommitted work' only for 'any other file true-up would remove' ([decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md)). In a scratch project, four uncommitted lines appended to `.claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md` drew 'DRIFT: stale: .claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md differs from the carried v26.0.0 rendering' and 'PLAN: 1 step(s), 0 destructive'; after the run the lines were in no file and not in HEAD. An owner who hand-edits a vendored rules file and upgrades before committing loses the edit.

The state of play. A removal of a suite file with an uncommitted change already moves the file into the archive. Stripping a retired layout from a file git cannot restore copies the file into the archive first and counts as destructive ([decision:retired-layout-strips-only-recoverable-files](.ok-planner/design/decisions/retired-layout-strips-only-recoverable-files.md)). A committed edit is safe, since git keeps it, and an unstamped vendored file with the same edit is archived under a destructive step. Only the rewrite of a stamped file with an uncommitted edit has no guard. The story and the two decisions cannot all hold for this file, and no stated rule says which gives way.

The ruling decides whether an uncommitted change in a stamped suite file makes its rewrite destructive.

recommendation.text:
Count a rewrite of a stamped suite file that carries an uncommitted or staged-only change as destructive. True-up copies the working file into the archive before it rewrites it, the plan marks the step destructive, and the owner's one consent covers it. A rewrite of a stamped file whose difference git holds in a commit stays a rewrite with no question.

Rationale: the story promises that an upgrade never costs the owner work they wrote, and the suite already keeps that promise for every other step that touches work git cannot restore: a removal archives such a file, and a retired-layout strip copies it into the archive first and asks. The consent rule uses the stamp to tell an untouched suite file from an edited one, and an appended edit leaves the stamp in place, so the stamp test misses the case the rule means to catch. A applies the suite's existing recoverability test to the one step that lacks it. B gives up the story for a file the owner can change with any editor. C keeps the text but moves a file into the archive without the consent the suite asks for every other archive move. D only reports the loss. The flip case: if owners in practice never hand-edit stamped files, and the uncommitted differences true-up meets are its own earlier output the owner has not yet committed, the question is noise, and D's report line would serve the owner as well at less cost.

title: True-up overwrites an uncommitted owner edit in a stamped suite file with no question and no copy
